blocks.text: Asthma is a **chronic inflammatory disease of the airways**. The inflammation makes the airways **hyper-responsive**, so patients get recurrent bouts of **wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough**, typically at **night and in the early morning**. The airflow obstruction is **widespread and variable**, and it often **reverses**, either on its own or with treatment.

blocks.title: The three defining features
items: **Airflow limitation** that is usually reversible (spontaneously or with treatment)
**Airway hyper-responsiveness (AHR)** to a wide range of stimuli
**Bronchial inflammation**: T lymphocytes, mast cells and eosinophils, with mucosal oedema, smooth-muscle hypertrophy, mucus plugging and epithelial damage

blocks.text: **Atopy** (a tendency to make IgE against common allergens) is strongly linked to asthma. Dendritic cells present allergen to **Th2 lymphocytes**, whose cytokines (IL-4 and IL-13 switch B cells to **IgE**; IL-5 and others support eosinophil and mast cell development) prime **mast cells**. Re-exposure triggers a biphasic response: an **early (type I) reaction** within minutes from release of pre-formed mediators (histamine, tryptase, PGD2, LTC4), then a **late-phase reaction** hours later driven by recruited inflammatory cells.

blocks.note: Look at: peak flow after allergen challenge, with an early dip (type I, pre-formed mediators) and a second, later dip from inflammatory cell recruitment.

blocks.title: What narrows the airway
items: Contraction of bronchial smooth muscle
Wall thickening from oedema and inflammatory cell infiltrate
Mucus and cell debris in the lumen
In chronic disease, **remodelling**: smooth-muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia, collagen laid down beneath the basement membrane, shedding of ciliated epithelium and more goblet cells

blocks.text: **AHR** means the airways narrow excessively in response to triggers that hardly affect a normal person. It is central to the diagnosis and is linked, though not exclusively, to airway inflammation.

Reversibility is not guaranteed for life. With increasing severity and duration, **remodelling** causes wall fibrosis and **fixed narrowing** with a smaller bronchodilator response, so incompletely reversible obstruction does not exclude long-standing asthma.

blocks.title: Triggers by group
rows: House-dust mite (the major allergen); pets such as cat, guinea pig, rabbit, horse; cockroaches and other pests; moulds after water damage; pollens
Viral upper respiratory tract infection: the **commonest trigger of exacerbations**
Exercise (especially in cold weather); cold, dry air

Tobacco smoke, car exhaust, solvents, strong perfumes, dust; pollution episodes (ozone, particulates, NO2, SO2) during temperature inversions; pollen surges after thunderstorms; moulds such as Alternaria and Cladosporium
Beta-blockers (even as eye drops), aspirin and other NSAIDs, the oral contraceptive pill, cholinergic agents, prostaglandin F2α
Isocyanates, flour and grain dust, colophony, latex, animal proteins (see Types of asthma)

blocks.text: **Exercise-induced** symptoms classically start **after**, not during, exertion. Hyperventilation dries the airway lining fluid (and cools the mucosa), which releases mediators from mast cells. FEV1 rises briefly at the end of exercise, then falls sharply and recovers slowly.

blocks.note: Look at: FEV1 after 6 minutes of exercise, with a small rise, then a sudden fall and gradual recovery over about 30 minutes.

blocks.text: **NSAIDs** (aspirin, propionic acid drugs such as ibuprofen, indometacin) worsen asthma in about **5%** of patients. Intolerance is most common in those who also have **nasal polyps**, and it often comes with rhinitis and flushing. Anyone intolerant of aspirin should avoid all NSAIDs.

**Beta-blockers**: even cardioselective drugs (atenolol) and topical eye drops can provoke attacks. Non-selective agents (propranolol) block the β2 effect of circulating adrenaline that normally offsets vagal bronchoconstriction, so the airflow limitation is seen only in asthmatics. Avoid beta-blockers in any form in asthma.
Exercise symptoms can be prevented by a proper **warm-up** or by taking a **β2-agonist, nedocromil or a leukotriene antagonist** beforehand.

blocks.title: Clinical types (phenotypes)
rows: Atopic child or young adult, often with eczema and hay fever
Positive skin-prick tests (about 90% of children and 70% of adults with persistent asthma)
Starts in middle age; attacks set off by respiratory infections
No atopy and no clear external trigger
Asthma + rhinosinusitis + nasal polyps; reacts to NSAIDs, sometimes alcohol and salicylate-rich foods
Better at weekends and on holiday
Cough is the main symptom, with little wheeze or breathlessness, so diagnosis is delayed
Symptoms brought on by exercise, especially in cold weather
Severe attacks with little or no warning

blocks.text: In **aspirin-sensitive asthma**, blocking cyclo-oxygenase diverts arachidonic acid down the **lipoxygenase pathway**, so more bronchoconstricting **cysteinyl leukotrienes** are made.

blocks.title: Inflammatory subtypes (induced sputum)
items: **Eosinophilic**: the usual pattern
**Neutrophilic**: seen in a severe form with less allergic drive, more common in women
**Pauci-granulocytic**: little inflammation of either kind

blocks.title: Occupational asthma
items: Suspect it in any **working-age adult with new-onset asthma** that improves away from work

Common agents: **isocyanates** (paint sprayers), **flour and grain dust** (bakers), colophony and fluxes (soldering), **latex** (nurses), animal proteins (laboratory animal workers), enzymes (laundry work)
Confirm with **serial peak flow at least 4 times a day for at least 3 weeks**, ideally including time away from work
Early removal from exposure may cure it
**Reactive airways dysfunction syndrome**: persistent asthma-like illness after a **single high-level irritant exposure** (gas, smoke, fumes)

blocks.note: Look at: serial peak flows that dip on working days and recover, with less diurnal variation, during time away from work.

blocks.title: "Asthma-plus" syndromes
rows: Asthma + hypersensitivity to Aspergillus + pulmonary infiltrates; affects about 1–2% of asthmatics

blocks.text: **Extrinsic** asthma is the atopic, IgE-driven type. **Intrinsic** asthma is, by definition, not linked to atopy, so do not expect it to come with high circulating IgE or positive skin tests.

blocks.title: Symptoms
items: Recurrent **wheeze, chest tightness, breathlessness and cough**
**Diurnal pattern**: worse at night and early morning; poor control disturbs sleep
Cough may be the only symptom, especially **nocturnal cough in children**
Upper-airway symptoms: sinusitis, blocked or runny nose, **loss of smell**
Mild intermittent asthma is usually symptom-free between episodes

blocks.title: Signs
items: Between attacks, examination is often **normal apart from wheeze**
Look for **nasal polyps** and **eczema**
A **vasculitic rash** suggests eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
In an attack: tachypnoea, tachycardia, accessory muscle use, reduced chest expansion, **prolonged expiration** and **widespread expiratory polyphonic wheeze**

blocks.text: **Variability** within and between days is the hallmark of asthma. A mild asthmatic may have no symptoms or signs when well, which contrasts with the steady, progressive disability of COPD. Childhood wheeze and atopy make asthma more likely.

blocks.title: Features that argue against asthma
items: Wheeze only with coughs and colds (viral-induced wheeze)
Isolated or productive cough
Normal investigations when symptomatic, and no response to treatment
**Unilateral wheeze**: think of a focal lesion or infection

blocks.title: "All that wheezes is not asthma"
items: Heart failure ("cardiac asthma")
COPD, bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease
Pulmonary embolism
Vocal cord dysfunction or upper-airway obstruction, inhaled foreign body
Panic and hyperventilation

blocks.text: In acute severe asthma, **paradoxical inward movement of the abdomen and diaphragm** on inspiration warns of impending respiratory failure.
Asthma is often misdiagnosed as a cold or a lingering chest infection (lasting more than about 10 days). Ask about the pattern, triggers and response to bronchodilators.

blocks.title: Making the diagnosis (Davidson): compatible history plus one of
rows: FEV1 up by **≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL** (more convincing if > 15% and > 400 mL)
**> 20% diurnal variation** on ≥ 3 days a week for 2 weeks
FEV1 falls by **≥ 15%** after 6 minutes of exercise

blocks.title: Spirometry and reversibility
items: Obstructive pattern: FEV1 reduced more than FVC, **FEV1/FVC < 0.70**; the flow–volume loop is "coved"
Repeat after salbutamol: a rise of **> 12% and > 200 mL** is significant reversibility; a large rise (> 400 mL) favours asthma
Spirometry can be **normal between episodes**

blocks.note: Look at: volume–time traces before and 20 minutes after a β2-agonist; FEV1 rises from 1.0 to 2.5 L, a positive reversibility test.
Look at: volume–time curves for normal, restrictive (FEV1 and FVC both reduced) and obstructive (essentially only FEV1 reduced) patterns.

blocks.title: Peak expiratory flow (PEF)
items: Record the **best of three** blows, morning and evening, and express it as % of predicted (from sex, height, age) or personal best
Asthma shows a **morning dip**; > 20% diurnal variation supports the diagnosis and its size reflects severity
Also used to grade control and acute severity

blocks.note: Look at: serial PEF chart with sharp overnight falls (morning dipping) that lessen once glucocorticoids are started.
Look at: PEF diary with early-morning dips that improve after a course of prednisolone.

blocks.title: Bronchial challenge (if lung function is normal)
items: Rising doses of **histamine, methacholine or mannitol**; result given as **PC20/PD20** (dose that drops FEV1 by 20%)
**High negative predictive value**, but positives also occur in COPD, bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis
Avoid if FEV1 < 1.5 L or there is a history of brittle asthma

blocks.note: Look at: % fall in FEV1 against rising histamine concentration; the curve shifts left (lower PC20) as asthma gets more severe.

blocks.title: Supporting tests
items: **FeNO ≥ 40 ppb** in a steroid-naive adult (marker of eosinophilic inflammation); NICE uses FeNO plus reversibility first-line
Atopy: **skin-prick tests** (weal read at 15 min) or total and specific IgE
Blood eosinophilia; **sputum eosinophilia is more specific**
Steroid trial (e.g. prednisolone 30 mg daily for 2 weeks) with improvement in FEV1 or PEF

blocks.title: Imaging and blood gases
items: **CXR is usually normal**; hyperinflation in an acute attack or severe disease
Lobar collapse from a mucus plug; **flitting infiltrates suggest ABPA**
CXR in an attack mainly excludes pneumothorax or pneumonia; HRCT detects bronchiectasis
ABG in an attack: hyperventilation normally gives a **low PaCO2**; a normal or rising PaCO2 means tiring

blocks.text: **Carbon monoxide transfer is normal in asthma.** A reduced TLCO in a patient with airflow obstruction points to emphysema instead.

Cut-offs differ between books: Kumar & Clark Essentials quotes ≥ 15% variability (and > 15% after a steroid trial). Davidson uses **≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL** for reversibility and **> 20%** for diurnal PEF variation, so use Davidson's figures in the exam.

blocks.title: Levels of asthma control
rows: **≥ 3 features of partly controlled asthma in any week**, or an exacerbation in that week

blocks.text: **Mild intermittent asthma**: symptoms under once weekly over 3 months, with under two nocturnal episodes per month. An as-required SABA is usually enough.

blocks.title: Start regular inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) if any of
items: An exacerbation in the last 2 years
β2-agonist use ≥ 3 times a week
Symptoms ≥ 3 times a week
Woken by asthma one night a week

blocks.title: Stepwise treatment (BTS/SIGN, as in Davidson)
rows: Move up if needed ≥ 3 times a week
Start about 400 µg BDP/day (more in smokers)
Add **LABA** to ICS, normally as a **combination inhaler**
No response: stop LABA and raise ICS. Partial response: keep LABA, raise ICS to medium dose
High-dose ICS (up to 2000 µg BDP/day) or a **fourth drug**
LTRA, SR theophylline, oral β2-agonist or LAMA; stop any add-on that does not help

blocks.note: Look at: the BTS/SIGN stepwise chart, moving up for poor control and down to the lowest therapy that keeps control.

blocks.text: Never give a **LABA alone** in asthma: monotherapy is linked to life-threatening attacks and asthma deaths. Fixed ICS/LABA inhalers prevent this and improve adherence. Adding a LABA beats raising the ICS dose alone.

blocks.title: Before stepping up and at every review
items: Check **adherence**, **inhaler technique** and ongoing **trigger exposure** (including smoking, which also causes relative steroid resistance)
Written self-management (action) plan, guided by PEF
Annual review and yearly influenza vaccine

blocks.note: Look at: metered-dose inhaler technique; shake, breathe out, slow deep breath in while pressing the canister, then hold the breath for 10 seconds.

blocks.title: Other drug points
items: **Budesonide/formoterol** can be both maintenance and reliever (MART), because formoterol acts as fast as salbutamol
**Montelukast 10 mg daily** is less effective than a LABA as add-on but can reduce ICS dose

Step 5 biologics: **omalizumab** (anti-IgE) for atopic disease; **mepolizumab/reslizumab** (anti-IL-5), **benralizumab** (anti-IL-5 receptor) for eosinophilic disease; dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα) and tezepelumab (anti-TSLP) are newer options
**Step down** once controlled: cut the steroid dose by about **25–50% every 3 months**

blocks.text: Ladders differ by guideline. **NICE 2017** adds an **LTRA before a LABA** and then considers MART. Kumar & Clark Essentials ties each step to PEF % predicted. The US NAEPP grades chronic severity (mild intermittent, mild/moderate/severe persistent). For the exam, follow the BTS/SIGN order above.

blocks.note: Look at: a stepwise adult asthma ladder (steps 1–6) linked to PEF % predicted.

blocks.title: Mild–moderate exacerbation at home
items: **Doubling the ICS dose does not prevent** an exacerbation
Give a rescue course of **prednisolone 30–60 mg daily**

Triggers for a rescue course: PEF falling day by day to **< 60% of personal best**, new or worse sleep disturbance, morning symptoms lasting until midday, a fading response to the inhaler, or needing nebulised/injected bronchodilator

blocks.text: In **pregnancy**, β2-agonists, ICS, theophyllines, oral prednisolone and chromones are safe. Women on prednisolone > 7.5 mg/day need **hydrocortisone 100 mg 3–4 times daily in labour**. Use prostaglandin F2α with great caution.

The books do not use the term "status asthmaticus". Its equivalent is **acute severe asthma**: an exacerbation that has not been controlled by standard medication. Davidson grades attacks as **acute severe**, **life-threatening** or **near-fatal**. It is a medical emergency, and in the UK about 1400 people die from asthma each year; most of these deaths are preventable.

blocks.title: Grading an acute attack (Davidson / BTS)
rows: PEF **33–50%** (< 200 L/min); HR **≥ 110**; RR **≥ 25**; cannot finish sentences in one breath
PEF **< 33%** (< 100 L/min); PaO2 < 8 kPa or SpO2 < 92%; **normal or raised PaCO2**; **silent chest**; cyanosis; feeble effort; bradycardia or arrhythmia; hypotension; exhaustion, delirium, coma
**Raised PaCO2** and/or needing mechanical ventilation with raised inflation pressures

blocks.text: Pocket Medicine uses **GINA** bands (severe = PEF ≤ 50%, RR > 30, HR > 120, talks in words). The cut-offs differ from Davidson's BTS bands (PEF 33–50%, RR ≥ 25, HR ≥ 110), so use Davidson's numbers in the exam.
**Pulsus paradoxus** is not a reliable severity marker (present in only about 45% of severe attacks). A **silent chest** is ominous: so little air moves that there is no wheeze.

blocks.title: Risk factors for a fatal attack
items: Previous intubation or near-fatal attack
Emergency visit or admission in the past year
Current or recent oral steroids; not using ICS; over-use of SABA
Psychiatric illness, poor adherence
Blunted perception of airway narrowing; brittle asthma

blocks.title: Immediate treatment
items: Measure **PEF** (unless too ill) and **ABG**; CXR only if pneumothorax is suspected
**High-flow oxygen** to keep SpO2 **> 92%**
**Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg** (or terbutaline), **oxygen-driven**; multiple puffs through a spacer work as well in primary care
Add **ipratropium 500 µg** in acute severe or life-threatening attacks
**Prednisolone 40 mg orally**, or **hydrocortisone 200 mg IV** if vomiting or unable to swallow
IV fluids if dehydrated; **replace potassium**

blocks.title: If the response is poor
items: Repeat nebulisers or give continuous salbutamol
**IV magnesium sulphate 1.2–2.0 g over 20 min** (mainly if presenting PEF < 30%)
IV aminophylline (with **cardiac monitoring**) or IV salbutamol
Inform ICU early; decide about intubation before the patient is exhausted

blocks.note: Look at: the acute asthma algorithm by PEF % predicted, with doses and admit/home decisions.
Look at: hospital flowchart for acute severe asthma covering initial treatment, escalation and discharge criteria.

blocks.text: **Oxygen targets differ**: Davidson keeps SpO2 **> 92%**, Kumar & Clark Essentials and Zero to Finals use 94–98%, and Step-Up uses > 90%. Whatever the target, a **high PaCO2 is never a reason to cut oxygen** in asthma; it signals a severe or life-threatening attack.
A "normal" PaCO2 in an attack is **not reassuring**. The patient should be hyperventilating with a low PaCO2, so a normal or rising level means tiring and impending respiratory failure.

blocks.title: Monitoring
items: PEF every 15–30 minutes, then every 4–6 hours
Pulse oximetry to keep SaO2 > 92%
Repeat ABG if the first PaCO2 was normal or raised, PaO2 < 8 kPa, or the patient worsens

blocks.title: Indications for intubation and ventilation
rows: PaO2 < 8 kPa and falling; PaCO2 > 6 kPa and rising; pH low and falling

blocks.text: When ventilating, use a large endotracheal tube, keep plateau pressure < 30 cm H2O and allow a long expiratory time to avoid air trapping. Heliox, inhalational anaesthetics and ECMO have been used in refractory cases.

blocks.title: Discharge
items: Stable on discharge medication, **off nebulisers for ≥ 24 hours**, PEF **≥ 75%** of predicted or best
Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days (some books give 40–50 mg for 7 days); start or increase ICS
Check technique, avoid triggers, **written self-management plan**
GP or asthma nurse review within **2 working days**; specialist clinic within a month
NICE suggests respiratory referral after **2 attacks in 12 months**

blocks.note: Look at: disposition after initial treatment of an exacerbation (home, ward or ICU).

blocks.text: **Antibiotics are not routine** in acute asthma: yellow or green sputum usually reflects eosinophils from a viral trigger, not bacteria.

sections.title: Complications of asthma & of its treatment

blocks.title: Complications of asthma
items: **Death or near-fatal attacks**, often in young people, usually from under-recognised severity and delayed treatment
**Respiratory failure** needing ventilation
**Pneumothorax** (asymmetric breath sounds, tracheal deviation, surgical emphysema) and **pneumomediastinum** (Hamman's precordial crunch)
**Lobar collapse** from mucus plugging
**ABPA** (about 1–2% of asthmatics): fever, cough with bronchial casts, flitting infiltrates, proximal bronchiectasis, total IgE > 417 kU/L, eosinophils > 0.5 × 10⁹/L
Fixed airflow obstruction from **remodelling**
In uncontrolled asthma in pregnancy: pre-eclampsia, hypertension, hyperemesis, haemorrhage; growth restriction, preterm birth, neonatal hypoxia, perinatal death

blocks.title: Adverse effects of asthma treatment
rows: Fine tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, headache, poor sleep; **hypokalaemia** at high doses
Monitor and replace K+ in acute asthma; caution in hyperthyroidism and arrhythmia
Higher risk of life-threatening attacks and asthma death
**Oral thrush, hoarseness**; rarely subcapsular cataract; osteoporosis at high dose; short-term growth slowing in children above 400 µg/day (final height unaffected)
Systemic side-effects (e.g. osteoporosis) if used > 3 months or > 3–4 courses a year
**Narrow therapeutic window** (10–20 mg/L): nausea, tachycardia, insomnia, arrhythmias, convulsions (especially with rapid IV dosing)
Levels (Davidson: 6 h post dose, steady state 2–3 days); cardiac monitoring with IV use; levels altered by smoking, liver disease, heart failure, interacting drugs
Dry mouth, tachycardia, constipation, **acute angle-closure glaucoma**
Shield eyes from nebulised drug; caution in prostatic enlargement

blocks.text: **Leukotriene receptor antagonists** (e.g. montelukast) carry a warning for serious neuropsychiatric effects, including suicide. Warn patients when starting one and ask about mood at review.

Inhaled steroids are absorbed. With a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as **ritonavir**, an inhaled steroid can cause **severe Cushing's syndrome** and HPA axis suppression. Systemic steroids can also alter mood and raise the neutrophil count.
Salbutamol drives potassium into cells, and steroids also lower potassium. In a patient on repeated nebulisers, **check U&E** and replace K+.
A **spacer** slows the aerosol so less drug lands in the mouth. It cuts the risk of candidiasis and helps patients who cannot coordinate the inhaler, such as children and older people.

cards.back: Reversible airflow limitation, airway hyper-responsiveness, and bronchial inflammation (T cells, mast cells, eosinophils).

cards.front: Two phases of the airway response to inhaled allergen?
cards.back: Early (type I) phase within minutes from pre-formed mast cell mediators, then a late phase hours later from recruited inflammatory cells.

cards.front: Why can long-standing asthma lose reversibility?
cards.back: Airway remodelling: wall fibrosis and smooth-muscle hypertrophy cause fixed narrowing and a smaller bronchodilator response.
Beta-blockers (even eye drops and cardioselective ones), aspirin/NSAIDs, oral contraceptive pill, cholinergic agents, prostaglandin F2α.
After exercise stops: FEV1 rises briefly, then falls sharply and recovers gradually. Cold air makes it worse.
Viral respiratory infection.
Asthma + aspirin/NSAID sensitivity + nasal polyps (with rhinosinusitis); classically a middle-aged woman.
Serial PEF at least 4 times a day for at least 3 weeks, ideally including time away from work.
Total IgE > 417 kU/L, eosinophils > 0.5 × 10⁹/L, Aspergillus sensitisation, proximal bronchiectasis.

cards.front: Wheeze feature that argues against asthma?
cards.back: Unilateral wheeze, which suggests a focal lesion or infection.

cards.front: Davidson's bronchodilator reversibility criterion for asthma?
cards.back: FEV1 rise ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL (more convincing if > 15% and > 400 mL).
> 20% on ≥ 3 days a week for 2 weeks, with the lowest values in the morning.

cards.front: Gas transfer (TLCO) in asthma vs emphysema?
cards.back: Normal in asthma (KCO normal or raised); markedly reduced in emphysema.

cards.front: When should regular ICS be started?
cards.back: Exacerbation in the last 2 years, SABA or symptoms ≥ 3 times a week, or night waking once a week.
≥ 3 features of partly controlled asthma in any week, or an exacerbation in that week.

cards.front: How fast should steroids be stepped down once asthma is controlled?
cards.back: Cut the dose by about 25–50% every 3 months to the lowest dose that keeps control.
PEF 33–50% predicted, HR ≥ 110, RR ≥ 25, unable to complete sentences in one breath.

cards.front: Blood gas findings that make an attack life-threatening?
cards.back: SpO2 < 92% or PaO2 < 8 kPa, or a normal or raised PaCO2.

cards.front: Dose of IV magnesium in acute severe asthma?
cards.back: 1.2–2.0 g IV over 20 minutes, if the response to initial treatment is poor.
Off nebulisers ≥ 24 h, stable on discharge drugs, PEF ≥ 75% of predicted or best; GP review within 2 working days.

cards.front: Electrolyte to monitor with repeated salbutamol?
cards.back: Potassium: salbutamol (and steroids) cause hypokalaemia.
10–20 mg/L, with a narrow margin before toxicity (arrhythmias, seizures).

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Water loss from the airway lining fluid

items.stem: A 25-year-old atopic volunteer inhales grass pollen extract in a research laboratory. His peak flow falls within 15 minutes and recovers by 2 hours. At 7 hours it falls again and stays low overnight. Which process explains the fall at 7 hours?
items.explanation: Two phases: the immediate fall is mast cell degranulation, but the second fall hours later comes from recruitment and activation of inflammatory cells (late-phase reaction).

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has had poorly treated asthma since childhood. She has never smoked. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC stays at 0.61 and FEV1 rises by only 4%. TLCO is normal and HRCT shows no emphysema.
items.explanation: Persistent obstruction with normal gas transfer in a lifelong asthmatic non-smoker points to remodelling (wall fibrosis, fixed narrowing) rather than emphysema.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man has episodic chest tightness, but his spirometry is normal today. Inhaled methacholine produces a 20% fall in FEV1 at a concentration that has no effect on healthy controls.
items.explanation: Excessive narrowing to a stimulus that barely affects normal airways is the definition of airway hyper-responsiveness.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with asthma that has been well controlled for years on a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid is reviewed 2 weeks after a myocardial infarction. Since discharge he has needed salbutamol several times a day. He has taken low-dose aspirin for 5 years without problems. Four new drugs were started in hospital.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is most likely to have caused his deterioration?
questions.explanation: Beta-blockers, including **cardioselective** ones such as atenolol, can provoke bronchospasm in asthma by blocking the β2 effect that opposes vagal bronchoconstriction. Aspirin has been tolerated for years, so NSAID sensitivity is not the issue.
whyNot: Statins are not a recognised asthma trigger.
Clopidogrel does not inhibit cyclo-oxygenase, so it does not shunt arachidonic acid to leukotrienes as aspirin can.
Calcium-channel blockers are not among the drugs that precipitate asthma.
Nitrates are not a recognised trigger of bronchospasm.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with asthma, well controlled on a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid, had 3 days of sore throat and runny nose. Her wheeze has since worsened and her peak flow has fallen to 65% of her best. She is afebrile and her chest X-ray is clear.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely precipitant of this exacerbation?
questions.explanation: Viral infections are the **commonest trigger of asthma exacerbations**. The coryzal prodrome followed by worsening wheeze is typical.
whyNot: No fever and a clear chest X-ray make pneumonia unlikely; discoloured sputum in asthma usually reflects eosinophils, not bacteria.
A perennial indoor allergen would not explain the coryzal prodrome.
Exercise causes short-lived wheeze just after exertion, not several days of worsening after a cold.
Cold air causes short-lived bronchoconstriction on exposure, not a days-long deterioration after a cold.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has a blocked nose, recurrent sinusitis and loss of smell. Within an hour of taking ibuprofen for back pain she became very wheezy. She also notices chest tightness after a glass of red wine.
items.explanation: Asthma with rhinosinusitis, nasal polyp symptoms (anosmia) and reactions to NSAIDs and alcohol is aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter's).

items.stem: A 34-year-old man started work in a car body shop 8 months ago. He now wheezes most evenings in the working week, and his symptoms settle during a 2-week holiday.
items.explanation: New adult asthma that improves away from work points to occupational asthma; isocyanates in spray paint are the classic cause.

items.stem: A 41-year-old maintenance worker with no previous chest disease was exposed to a large chlorine gas leak while cleaning a tank. Six months later he still has cough, wheeze and a positive methacholine challenge, regardless of whether he is at work.
items.explanation: Two steps: the illness is work-related, but it began after one massive irritant exposure, not gradual sensitisation, and does not vary with work. This is reactive airways dysfunction syndrome.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is referred with a label of "asthma". Several features of his history are listed.
questions.leadIn: Which feature most strongly argues against asthma?
options: Wheeze heard only over the right lower chest
A dry cough that wakes him at night
Symptoms that are worst on waking
Chest tightness after stroking a cat
questions.explanation: **Unilateral wheeze** suggests a focal lesion (e.g. an obstructing tumour or foreign body) or localised infection, not diffuse airway disease.
whyNot: Nocturnal cough fits the diurnal pattern of asthma.
Early-morning symptoms are typical of asthma.
Wheeze after allergen exposure supports allergic asthma.
A history of atopy makes asthma more likely.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with adult-onset asthma reports a constantly blocked nose, recurrent sinus infections and loss of smell. Last year she became very wheezy after taking ibuprofen.
questions.leadIn: Which examination finding is most likely?
questions.explanation: Davidson advises inspecting for **nasal polyps** in asthma. Anosmia, sinus disease and NSAID sensitivity make polyps very likely (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease).
whyNot: Clubbing is not a feature of asthma and suggests another diagnosis.
Fine crackles suggest fibrosis or heart failure.
A fixed localised wheeze suggests a focal obstruction.
Tracheal deviation suggests pneumothorax or collapse, not this chronic picture.

questions.theme: Interpreting lung function in a breathless patient
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Reversible airflow obstruction typical of asthma
Airflow obstruction with reduced gas transfer (emphysema)
Restrictive defect with reduced gas transfer (fibrosis)
Airflow obstruction without significant reversibility, normal gas transfer

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has FEV1 1.60 L and FEV1/FVC 0.58. Twenty minutes after salbutamol her FEV1 is 2.15 L.
items.explanation: FEV1 rose by 550 mL (about 34%), well above the 12% and 200 mL threshold, so the obstruction is reversible.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man who has smoked 45 pack-years has FEV1/FVC 0.52 with a 3% rise after salbutamol. TLCO and KCO are both markedly reduced.
items.explanation: Fixed obstruction with low gas transfer points to emphysema; TLCO is normal in asthma.

items.stem: A 30-year-old teacher has episodic night cough and wheeze. Spirometry today is normal, but FEV1 falls by 20% at a low concentration of inhaled histamine.
items.explanation: When baseline spirometry is normal, a low PC20 on bronchial challenge shows hyper-responsiveness and supports asthma.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man records peak flows for 2 weeks. On 4 days each week his morning reading is about 300 L/min and his evening reading about 420 L/min.
items.explanation: Morning dips with variation of more than 20% on at least 3 days a week for 2 weeks meet Davidson's diary criterion.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman uses a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid. In the past week she had daytime symptoms on 4 days, woke once with cough, and used salbutamol 4 times. She has not limited her activities, her PEF is 92% of her best, and she has had no exacerbation this year.
questions.leadIn: How should her current asthma control be classified?
questions.explanation: Count the partly-controlled features in that week: daytime symptoms > 2/week, **any** night waking, reliever > 2/week. **Three features in one week = uncontrolled.**
whyNot: Controlled requires no night symptoms and reliever use ≤ 2/week.
Partly controlled means fewer than 3 such features in the week; she has 3.
Mild intermittent means symptoms less than weekly, which is not the case.
Acute severe is an emergency grade (PEF 33–50%, tachycardia, unable to complete sentences), not a control level.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man still has symptoms most days despite beclometasone 400 µg daily. His inhaler technique and adherence are good and he has no ongoing trigger exposure.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step according to the BTS/SIGN approach in Davidson?
options: Add a LABA as an ICS/LABA combination inhaler
Replace the ICS with salmeterol alone
Stop the ICS and use salbutamol as needed
questions.explanation: Step 3 is to add a **LABA**, normally in a **combination inhaler**. This gives better control than raising the ICS dose, and the combined device stops LABA being used alone.
whyNot: LABA monotherapy is linked to life-threatening attacks and asthma death.
Daily oral steroid is step 5, after add-on options fail.
Biologics are reserved for step 5 disease.
This steps down treatment in someone who is uncontrolled.

questions.theme: Severity of acute presentations in asthma
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has a PEF of 45% of predicted, respiratory rate 28/min and pulse 116/min. She cannot finish a sentence in one breath. SpO2 is 95% on air.
items.explanation: PEF 33–50%, RR ≥ 25, HR ≥ 110 and broken sentences, with no life-threatening feature, define acute severe asthma.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man is drowsy with a quiet chest on auscultation. PEF is 25% of predicted, SpO2 90% on oxygen and PaCO2 5.2 kPa.
items.explanation: Two steps: PEF < 33%, SpO2 < 92% and a silent chest are life-threatening features; the "normal" PaCO2 is also life-threatening because he should be blowing it off.

items.stem: A 19-year-old with a severe attack deteriorates despite maximal treatment. She is intubated in the emergency department and needs high inflation pressures to ventilate.
items.explanation: Raised PaCO2 and/or needing mechanical ventilation with raised inflation pressures defines near-fatal asthma.

items.stem: During an acute attack, a 27-year-old man suddenly develops right-sided chest pain. He has no breath sounds over the right hemithorax, and his trachea has shifted towards the left.
items.explanation: Barotrauma: asymmetric breath sounds with tracheal deviation suggest a pneumothorax; a crunching sound over the heart would suggest pneumomediastinum instead.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman started beclometasone by metered-dose inhaler 2 months ago. She now has a hoarse voice and white plaques on her palate that scrape off.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Use a spacer and rinse her mouth after each dose
Replace the steroid with a LABA inhaler alone
questions.explanation: Oral candidiasis and dysphonia are local effects of ICS. A **spacer** slows the aerosol so less drug lands in the mouth, and **rinsing after use** removes the rest.
whyNot: ICS is still needed for control; local side-effects can be prevented.
Oral steroid adds systemic toxicity to treat a local problem.
LABA alone is dangerous in asthma.
A higher dose would worsen local side-effects.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with asthma and heart failure takes sustained-release theophylline as a step 4 add-on. He presents with nausea, palpitations and a first generalised seizure.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation should be done first to confirm the likely cause?
questions.explanation: Theophylline has a **narrow therapeutic range (10–20 mg/L)**. Toxicity causes nausea, tachyarrhythmias and convulsions, and levels vary considerably with heart failure, liver disease, smoking and interacting drugs.
whyNot: IgE helps assess atopy, not drug toxicity.
A CXR does not explain this triad of gastrointestinal, cardiac and neurological symptoms.
FeNO measures airway inflammation.
Skin tests look for allergic triggers.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 52-year-old non-atopic man has severe asthma despite high-dose ICS, a LABA and maintenance oral prednisolone. Skin-prick tests are negative, total IgE is normal and his blood eosinophil count is persistently high.
items.explanation: Step 5 disease with eosinophilic, non-atopic inflammation: anti-IL-5 (mepolizumab). Omalizumab targets IgE in atopic disease.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman with acute asthma has had high-flow oxygen, two oxygen-driven nebulisers of salbutamol with ipratropium, and prednisolone 40 mg. Thirty minutes later her PEF is 28% of predicted.
items.explanation: Poor response with presenting PEF < 30%: IV magnesium sulphate 1.2–2.0 g over 20 minutes.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man with acute severe asthma is vomiting repeatedly and cannot keep tablets down.
items.explanation: All acute severe attacks need systemic steroid; IV hydrocortisone (200 mg) is used when the oral route fails.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman on budesonide wants a once-daily tablet add-on. She has exercise-induced symptoms and nasal polyps with aspirin sensitivity.
items.explanation: A leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast 10 mg daily) is the oral add-on and works especially well in aspirin-sensitive and exercise-induced asthma.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has episodic wheeze. Baseline FEV1 is 2.10 L with FEV1/FVC 0.66. Several possible results are listed.
questions.leadIn: Which result best confirms asthma by Davidson's criteria?
options: FEV1 rises to 2.55 L after salbutamol
FEV1 rises to 2.20 L after salbutamol
FEV1 rises by 4% after a 2-week steroid trial
FEV1 falls by 5% after 6 minutes of exercise
PEF varies by 8% between morning and evening
questions.explanation: A rise of 450 mL (about 21%) clears the **≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL** threshold and even the > 400 mL "greater confidence" level.
whyNot: A 100 mL (~5%) rise is below threshold.
A 4% steroid response is not significant.
The exercise criterion is a fall of ≥ 15%.
Diurnal PEF variation needs to exceed 20%.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old ex-smoker has airflow obstruction on spirometry. You need to decide between asthma and emphysema.
questions.leadIn: Which finding on full lung function testing most strongly favours emphysema?
questions.explanation: **Gas transfer is normal in asthma** but markedly reduced in emphysema, where alveolar destruction removes capillary surface area.
whyNot: Residual volume can be raised in both from air trapping.
A reduced ratio occurs in any obstructive disease.
A normal or raised KCO fits asthma.
A normal TLC fits asthma; emphysema usually raises TLC, so this does not favour emphysema.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with acute asthma is on high-flow oxygen. SpO2 is 93%, PEF 30% of predicted, and arterial PaCO2 6.4 kPa.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate response to the blood gas result?
options: Continue high-flow oxygen and seek urgent intensive care review
Reduce oxygen to 24% by Venturi mask
Wait for a chest X-ray before treating further
questions.explanation: A raised PaCO2 in asthma marks a **tiring patient with a near-fatal attack**; it is a warning sign, **not** a reason to cut oxygen. Escalate early because intubation may be needed.
whyNot: Controlled oxygen is for CO2-retaining COPD; in asthma reducing oxygen worsens hypoxia.
Bronchodilators should be intensified, not stopped.
Antibiotics are not routine in acute asthma.
CXR is only urgent if pneumothorax is suspected; treatment must not wait.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is recovering on the ward after admission with acute severe asthma.
questions.leadIn: Which criterion should be met before she is discharged?
options: Off nebulisers for ≥ 24 hours with PEF ≥ 75% of predicted or best
PEF ≥ 50% of predicted on the morning of discharge
Completion of 5 days of IV hydrocortisone
questions.explanation: Davidson's discharge criteria: stable on discharge drugs, **nebulisers stopped for at least 24 hours**, and **PEF ≥ 75%** of predicted or personal best, plus a written plan and early follow-up.
whyNot: 50% is still in the acute severe/moderate range.
An SpO2 of 88% would be hypoxic for an asthmatic.
Oral prednisolone is usual; IV steroid is not required.
CXR is often normal and is not a discharge criterion.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with acute asthma has received high-flow oxygen, two nebulisers of salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 500 µg, and prednisolone 40 mg orally. Thirty minutes later she is alert but her PEF is 27% of predicted and SpO2 is 94%.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next drug?
options: IV magnesium sulphate 1.2–2.0 g over 20 minutes
questions.explanation: Step 1: grade her. PEF < 33% makes this **life-threatening** asthma. Step 2: check first-line treatment is done: oxygen, oxygen-driven SABA + ipratropium, systemic steroid. Step 3: escalate for a poor response. **IV magnesium** gives extra bronchodilation, especially with PEF < 30%; aminophylline or IV salbutamol and early ICU input are other options.
whyNot: Antibiotics are not routine in acute asthma.
An LTRA is a maintenance add-on, not rescue therapy.
A LABA has no role in acute rescue, and should never be used alone.
Biologics are long-term step 5 treatment, not for acute attacks.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old baker has had wheeze for 9 months. It is worst late in the working week and improves when he is on holiday. Spirometry in clinic today is borderline.
questions.leadIn: Which test is best to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
options: Serial PEF ≥ 4 times daily for ≥ 3 weeks, including time away from work
A single spirometry test on a Monday morning
questions.explanation: Step 1: new adult asthma that improves away from work suggests **occupational asthma** (flour dust in a baker). Step 2: show the link objectively. **Serial peak flows** at least 4 times a day for at least 3 weeks, at work and away from it, show the work-related pattern.
whyNot: One reading cannot show the pattern linked to work.
CXR is usually normal in asthma.
Total IgE shows atopy, not a link to the workplace.
HRCT looks for bronchiectasis, not occupational triggers.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man on an ICS/LABA inhaler has had worsening asthma for 4 days. His PEF has fallen each day and is now 55% of his best. He wakes every night, and his morning symptoms last until midday. He can talk in full sentences, his pulse is 96/min and his respiratory rate is 18/min.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: A short rescue course of oral prednisolone 30–60 mg daily
questions.explanation: Step 1: exclude acute severe asthma: he has no severe features. Step 2: recognise the rescue-course triggers: PEF falling to **< 60% of best**, new night waking, morning symptoms until midday. Step 3: Davidson notes that **doubling ICS does not prevent** an exacerbation, so give a short course of **prednisolone 30–60 mg**.
whyNot: Doubling ICS has been shown not to prevent an impending exacerbation.
An LTRA is a slow-acting maintenance add-on.
Biologics are for persistent step 5 disease, not a single exacerbation.
Most exacerbations are viral; antibiotics are not indicated.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with mild asthma was started on timolol drops for open-angle glaucoma 3 weeks ago. His asthma has been much worse since.
items.explanation: Topical beta-blockers are absorbed systemically and can provoke bronchospasm.

items.stem: A 22-year-old cross-country runner gets chest tightness about 10 minutes after finishing winter training runs. She is fine while actually running.
items.explanation: Wheeze that comes after exertion, made worse by cold dry air, is exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with asthma has a postpartum haemorrhage. Shortly after a prostaglandin uterotonic is injected she becomes acutely wheezy.
items.explanation: Two steps: identify the drug as a prostaglandin used for uterine atony, then recall that prostaglandin F2α can induce bronchospasm and must be used with great caution in asthma.

items.stem: A 29-year-old theatre nurse has developed itchy hands under her gloves and, more recently, wheeze during shifts that settles on days off.
items.explanation: Glove-related skin reactions plus work-related wheeze in a nurse point to latex sensitisation.

questions.theme: Next step in long-term asthma management
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Add a LABA as a combination inhaler
Stop the LABA and increase the ICS dose
Trial of a fourth drug (LTRA, LAMA or SR theophylline)
Lowest-dose daily oral prednisolone with specialist care
Check adherence and inhaler technique first
Start a LABA on its own

items.stem: A 24-year-old man uses salbutamol 4 times a week and is woken by asthma about once a week. He takes no other treatment.
items.explanation: Reliever use or symptoms ≥ 3 times a week, or weekly night waking, are indications for regular ICS (step 2).

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has been well controlled for 4 months on beclometasone 800 µg daily with salmeterol. She has had no exacerbations.
items.explanation: Once control is stable, step down by cutting the steroid dose by about 25–50% every 3 months.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man on ICS/LABA reports poor control. His repeat prescriptions were collected only every 3 months for a monthly inhaler, and he fires the inhaler after he has finished breathing in.
items.explanation: Two steps: the records show under-use and the description shows poor technique. Fix adherence and technique before any step-up.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman had a LABA added to her low-dose ICS 8 weeks ago. Her adherence and technique are good, but her symptoms and peak flows are no better at all.
items.explanation: No response to a LABA: stop it and consider increasing the ICS dose.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps becomes severely wheezy within an hour of taking aspirin.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best explains her reaction?
options: Cyclo-oxygenase inhibition diverting arachidonic acid to cysteinyl leukotriene production
IgE antibodies against aspirin triggering mast cell degranulation
Water loss from the airway lining fluid
questions.explanation: With cyclo-oxygenase blocked, arachidonic acid is shunted down the **lipoxygenase pathway**, increasing bronchoconstricting **cysteinyl leukotrienes**. That is why leukotriene antagonists work well in this group.
whyNot: The reaction is pharmacological, not an IgE allergy to aspirin.
This is how beta-blockers trigger asthma.
This is how cholinergic agents and methacholine act.
This is how exercise triggers bronchospasm.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old non-smoker has had 4 months of dry cough at night and after going out into cold air. She has no wheeze or breathlessness. Chest X-ray and spirometry are normal. A methacholine challenge is positive, and the cough settles with an inhaled corticosteroid.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: When **cough is the dominant symptom** without wheeze or breathlessness, asthma is easily missed. Airway hyper-responsiveness and a steroid response confirm cough-variant asthma.
whyNot: Bronchiectasis causes a chronic productive cough.
COPD needs fixed obstruction, usually in a smoker.
Viral wheeze is wheeze with colds, not a months-long cough with hyper-responsiveness.
Vocal cord dysfunction is an asthma mimic that would not respond to ICS.

questions.theme: Complications of asthma and its treatment
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Acute angle-closure glaucoma from nebulised antimuscarinic

items.stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV takes a ritonavir-boosted regimen and fluticasone for asthma. Over 3 months he develops a round face, purple striae and proximal weakness.
items.explanation: Ritonavir blocks CYP3A4, so inhaled fluticasone accumulates and causes iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has had salbutamol nebulisers every 30 minutes for an acute attack. She now feels weak and has palpitations, and her serum potassium is 2.9 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Repeated β2-agonist drives potassium into cells (steroids add to the loss). Monitor and replace K+.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman admitted with acute asthma is given nebulised ipratropium through a face mask. Hours later she has a painful red eye, blurred vision and haloes around lights.
items.explanation: Nebulised antimuscarinic reaching the eye can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma; shield the eyes.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man with long-standing asthma has fevers and coughs up bronchial casts. CXR shows shifting infiltrates and CT shows proximal bronchiectasis. Total IgE is 1500 kU/L and eosinophils 1.2 × 10⁹/L.
items.explanation: Two steps: the casts, flitting infiltrates and proximal bronchiectasis suggest an asthma-plus syndrome, and very high IgE with eosinophilia confirms ABPA.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with severe asthma takes maintenance prednisolone 10 mg daily. She is admitted in established labour.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate steroid management during labour?
options: Double the inhaled steroid dose only
Give a single dose of oral prednisolone 5 mg
questions.explanation: Women taking **more than 7.5 mg/day** of prednisolone need **hydrocortisone 100 mg 3–4 times daily** in labour to cover the stress response.
whyNot: Stopping long-term steroid risks adrenal insufficiency.
Inhaled steroid gives no systemic stress cover.
Her dose exceeds the 7.5 mg/day threshold for cover.
This dose is less than her usual maintenance and gives no stress cover.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man with previous myocardial infarction has 3 weeks of breathlessness lying flat, waking at night gasping, and wheeze. He has ankle oedema and bibasal crackles.
items.explanation: Orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, oedema and crackles in a man with ischaemic heart disease: heart failure can cause wheeze ("cardiac asthma").

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman developed asthma last year. She now has a vasculitic rash on her legs and a blood eosinophil count of 4.0 × 10⁹/L.
items.explanation: Asthma plus marked eosinophilia plus a vasculitic rash is eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Churg–Strauss).

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has had a wheeze heard only over the right lower zone since choking on a peanut at a party 2 weeks ago.
items.explanation: Localised (unilateral) wheeze after a choking episode suggests an inhaled foreign body, not asthma.

ospe.identify: Biphasic peak-flow response to allergen: early (type I) dip from pre-formed mast cell mediators, then a late-phase dip hours later from inflammatory cell recruitment.
Exercise-induced asthma: FEV1 rises briefly at the end of exercise, then falls sharply and recovers gradually.
Occupational asthma: peak flows fall on working days and recover, with less diurnal variation, during time away from work.
Positive reversibility test: FEV1 rises from 1.0 to 2.5 L 20 minutes after a β2-agonist (≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL).
Asthma peak-flow diary: marked morning dipping (> 20% diurnal variation) that improves after glucocorticoids are started.
Bronchial challenge: % fall in FEV1 against rising histamine dose; more severe asthma reaches a 20% fall (PC20) at a lower concentration.
Volume–time spirograms: airflow limitation (essentially only FEV1 reduced, so the FEV1/FVC ratio falls) versus a restrictive pattern (FEV1 and FVC both reduced).
